newsitem.title: USA: Maine to give voters a choice on timber measure.
newsitem.headline: Maine to give voters a choice on timber measure.

text.p: Maine's Senate over the weekend followed the lead of the House and agreed to put a second, less radical choice on clear-cutting that was proposed by the governor before the voters in a November referendum.

A spokesman for Gov. Angus King said that two amendments that King had objected to, which would have added seven new forestry jobs and given the legislature the right to appoint four of seven members of a control board, were stripped.

King's proposal, which will compete with one proposed by the Green Party, would restrict clear-cutting to a 75-acre swath instead of the current 250-acre limit. The Green Party would totally ban this method of harvesting trees.
However, Maine voters also will have the right to reject both proposals, which were agreed at a special session called to approve the governor's bill.

The House and Senate also approved legislation that will make technical changes to allow the state to accept block welfare grants, saving it from the risk of losing from $9 to $12 million in federal funds. The new federal welfare bill relies heavily on giving the states block grants.
Another bill to help save 450 jobs at the C.F. Hathaway Co shirt factory in Waterville was substantially altered at the last minute, said the governor's spokesman, Dennis Bailey.

The new measure, which was signed by King on Monday morning, would use the Rainy Day Fund to give a new investor group $150,000 a year for 10 years to buy the factory's capital equipment, Bailey said.

A fourth bill, which would let the employers of workers who rely on tips, like restaurants, to continue to include estimated tips as part of the minimum wage they pay their workers receive, was approved by the legislature.

But the governor might not sign the measure into law because it would not go into effect until December. That means the workers would only get most of the benefit of the rise in the federal minimum wage, which starts in October, for two months. "The governor has some real concerns about that," said Bailey.
